1 2 C O U N C I L . The motion carried, and the Council proceeded to the Hall of Representatives . HALL HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, Wednesday, Dec. 5th, 1866, 7 o'clock, P. M. Iu pursuance of a resolution of invitation passed by the House of Representatives, inviting the Council to assemble in theirHall injoint convention for the purpose of receiving the message of his Excellency, Governor D. W. BALLARD, the two houses assembled, Hon. Geo. Ainslie, President of the Council, in the Chair. Street of the Council, and Parkinson of the House, were appointed as the committee. The committee, with the Governor, were announced. The Governor was introduced to the President of the Convention by Mr. Street, when he proceeded to deliver his annual mes- sage, as follows : G O V E R N O R ' S M E S S A G E . EXECUTIVE DEPARTMENT, Gentlemen of the Council and House of Representatives : In obedience to the requirements of established custom, I present to your Honorable body the Message expected to be read at the opening of your session. To the greater portion of the population of our Territory, the year now closing has been a year of prosperity. Many who began the year with perplexing doubts and misgivings as to the future of the country,have had those doubts and anxie- ties happily removed, and the success of the past leads them to hope and trust for the future. W e have been spared the calamities of famine and pesti- lence, while the benign blessingsof peace, health and abund- ance have been bestowed upon us by a kind and overruling Providence with an unsparing measure. These signal marks of God's good providence shouldcall out our deepest gratitude

# Page 18^page=18
J O U R N A L . 1 3 toHim whose good pleasure it has been thus to prosper and bless us as a people. For the first two years after the settlementof our Territory, Idaho was looked upon only as a theater for speculation and as a place for a temporary residence, where, by enduring the necessary toil and privations,rapid fortunes might be acquired. The Territory was first peopled by those whose object was the acquirement of a speedy fortune,and thisbeing done to return either to the Pacific or Atlantic States ; but this feeling is rap- idly subsiding and the abundant success attending both mining and agricultural pursuits during the past year is fast removing the prejudices thathave formerly existed againstIdaho asbeing a desirable location for a permanent residence. The most reliable information on the subject establishes the fact, that the yield of precious metals, in the aggregate,for the past year exceeds that of any preceding year. This, in con- nection with the fact that operations in gold and silver quartz, our principal source of mineral wealth, are as yet only in em- bryo, is a source of gratification to every one concerned in the future prosperity of the Territory. The ledges already opened and worked uniformly present indications of increasing rich- ness ; in not a single instance have there been indications of depreciation in the deposits of mineral wealth. Only a small proportion of the gold and silver bearing quartz ledges already discovered and known to be rich, some of them almost fabu- lously so, are as yet being worked. From observations made during the past summer by intelligent and scientificgentlemen, the conclusion is drawn that these ledges, which have yielded so abundantly during the present year, will next year produce still greater profits, while many more will be successfully opened and their yield be found to be equally abundant. Agriculturalpursuits, for two years almosttotallyneglected, have been prosecuted during the past year with the most grat- ifying results. Many hundreds of acres, in the Boise Valley and other localities, have been brought under cultivation, and it is cheering to learn that the yield per acre, of both cereals and vegetables, will compare favorably with the yield of any other locality on the Pacific coast. The day is not fardistant whenbut little if any of the productions raised on the Pacific coast will be brought over the Blue Mountains for the support of the people of Idaho Territory. Arrangements for more extended operations inboth mining and agricultural pursuits are already inprogress for the ensuing year. The amount of land cultivatedthis year will doubtlessbe more than doubled next, and it issafe to estimate that equal successcess will attend the mining interests of the country. In connectionwiththe agri- }

# Page 19^page=19
1 4 C O U N C I L . " cultural interests of the Territory it is not uninteresting to know, that an enterprising farmer of Boise Valley,during the past summer, cultivated sorghum with the most successful re- sults. While the two principal pursuits of our Territory, mining and agricultural,have thus been prosecuted with efficient en- ergy and success, all other industrial pursuits consequent upon them have been correspondingly remunerative, and it isbe- lieved that there are more settled families, more competent business men, more active and worthy working men, such as constitute the bone and sinew of every country, now in our midst who look upon Idaho as their future home, than there ever have been at any previous period. The idea of extravagant speculation isgiving way to patient toil and well regulatedeconomy, and judging the futureby the past, this healthier sentiment on the part of the people will gradually increase until Idaho will abound in all the fixtures and elements of a well established and properly organized com- munity. As the resources of the country are more and more developed, other branches of industry, hitherto dormant, will doubtless be thrown open for the active and energetic labor of the country. All things considered, the future of Idaho may now be looked upon with more confidence than at any former • period of her history. One fact connected with our business relations is a source of just pride to our citizens. Our merchants command a respect in the commercial circles of the coast not surpassed by the mer- chants of any other community. After a careful examination of the facts, it is believed that the wholesale merchants of our commercial ports, whose patronage has been extended to the merchants of Idaho, have sustained less lossthrough them than through the merchants of any other community where the same amount of business has been transacted. When we con- sider the vast amount of trade that has passed through the hands of our merchants, our great distance fromthe seaboard, the extended ranges ofmountains over which our routes of land carriagemust necessarily pass, and the consequent perplexities attending the delivery of goods in ourtowns,and the very few failures experienced, we may indeed point with just pride to the character of our merchants as men of fine business qualifi cations, and to the resources of our country as inexhaustible. Another source of congratulation to our citizens, is to be found in themarked decrease of crime in our midst. During the past year but few casesofmurder or highway robberyhave occurred,while during the same time crimes of sinaller grade have evidently been on the decrease. -

# Page 20^page=20
J O U R N A L . 1 5 It is to be hoped that in all coming time the arm of the law inIdaho will be sufficiently powerful for the protection of her citizens inboth life and property, and that whatever may have been the apparent provocations in times past,no such apparent necessity will ever again exist,and that it will not in the future be necessary for citizens, in their own name and without the authority of law, to undertake the administration of justice. No instance of dissatisfaction to the people has occurred during the past year from the regular operations of the law. Where crimes have been committed, the parties accused of the same have, in due time,been put upon trial, and the people have heartily acquiesced in the result. Everywhere in our Territory the increased promptness and stability of our courts is looked upon as a just source of increased confidence, on the part of the people. Therefore, with regrets for any deplorable events thatmay have occurred in the past,we may rejoice over the brighter prospect for the future. With regard to legislation to be done at the present session, I have but few recommendations to make . Indeed it seems to me that no great amount of legislation is at present required. It is thought that familiarity with the existing statutes is of greater consequence to the people than increased legislation. While it is important that needed changes inthe laws should, from time to time,be made, and necessary new ones enacted, it is equally important that the statutes should remain free from complications by amendment, at least long enough for thepeople to become familiar with them and their practical workings. Since the adjournment of the last Legislature the laws en- acted at that and the preceding session have been printed, in separate volumes,each of which has been appropriately and conveniently indexed. The publishing work has been well executed, in good type and on good paper, with substantial binding, but for want of funds to pay for the work the books still remain in the hands of the Publishers at San Francisco. The embarrassment under which you must necessarily labor in not having these laws before you are fully appreciated, as with- out them it is impossible that your present legislation can be performed understandingly or with as much satisfaction,either to yourselves or to your constituents, as could be done, could access be had to these bound volumes. In fact,the statutes of theTerritoryare in avery unsatisfactorycondition. The firstLegislature, which assembled at Lewiston in 1863, enacted a code,but as the duration of their session was lim- ited, itwas necessarily passed in much haste, and with much less consideration than its importance demanded. The code

# Page 21^page=21
1 6 C O U N C I L . 1 then enacted was not printed until after the sitting ofthe next Legislature, and many of the amendments have never been publishedin any form whatever, and indeed each succeeding Legislature has labored under the misfortune of endeavoring to amend the legislation of its predecessor with no authentic knowledge on the subject matter. The result is, that our laws are inharmonious and abound in perplexing discrepancies. It is believed that the best method of securing a perfect code of laws,and remedying the existing evils, is by the appointment of a commission to codify and revise the whole body of our statutes. The present uncertainty can thus be remedied by a system which, though itmay take some time and incur some expense, will, when complete, supersede for years the necessity of further amendments and additional legislation. ; Your attention is called to the fact that the hostile Indians still continue to harrass our routes of travel and frontier set- tlements, making it unsafe for prospecting parties to explore many portions of our country, except in large numbers, well- armed ; thus retarding the development of our country. In view of these facts, I recommend the passage of an Act for the organization of the Militia of the Territory. The want of arms for protection against thesehostile bands is severely felt by our citizens. The organization of the Militiawould not only serve to place us in a better condition for defense against the savages, but would also entitle us to our quota of arms from the Government. With a good supply of arms in their hands it is believed that our citizens would, in a short time, be able to bring to terms of peace the few marauding bands of Indians that infest our borders,committing with somuch ap- parent impunity their predatory attacks upon the unwary traveler and settler. The financial affairs of the Territory are far from being in a satisfactory condition, as may be seen by an examination of the Reports of the Territorial Treasurer and Controller. The rèmedy suggested is in the most rigid economy and athorough and stringent revenue law. No one should desire or be per- mitted to live in a country where he can claim the protection and benefit of its laws, and at the same time refuse to be laid under contribution to sustain thatcountry and support itslaws. Since allgood citizens willinglypay their taxes, ititisbutjustice to them that all should be made equally to assist in the burden of taxation . Could all the taxes due from our citizens have been promptly collected and paid into the Treasury, even at existing rates, doubtless our revenue would have been quite sufficient for all the expenditures of the Territory. Since the passage of the Organic Act, Congress has made )

# Page 22^page=22
J O U R N A L . 1 7 an annual appropriation of $20,000 to defray the legislative expenses ofthe Territory, and the sum of$1,000 for incidental expenses. From the records now on filein the Territorial Sec- retary's Office, it is ascertained that ofthe $84,000 thus appro- priated for this and the three years' preceding, only $9,983 00 have been received and expended in accordance with the objects of the appropriations. I need scarcely call your attention to the factthat this appropriation is by far too small for the ob- jects specified, and I would recommend that a memorial be addressed to Congress on this subject, soliciting that body to make the next appropriation in accordance with the estimate of our Territorial Secretary,now on file in the Treasury De- partment at Washington, and to appoint a special commission, fully authorized and empowered to investigate and adjust the claims now existing against the Government arising from leg- islative and incidental expenses. It is befitting that I should allude to the great importance of a railroad communication from the navigable waters of the Columbia river, via Boise Valley, to the Salt Lake Valley, in- tersecting the Central Pacific railway at some point in that region. A Bill, contemplating the establishment ofsuch a road, was brought before the last session of Congress. It passed the Senate and was referred to the Committee on the Pacific Rail- road by the House of Representatives, and will probably be- come a law during the present session of Congress. The im- portance of the enterprise is so deeply felt by every citizen of Idaho as to render it unnecessary for me to urge your hearty co-cperation with the Government in carrying forward the design. Our common schools are not in so flourishing a condition as could be desired. The apparent want of interest on this sub- ject has grown out of the unsettled condition of many of our citizens, who, expecting to remain but a short time in Idaho, havegiven attentionmore to other subjects than to the educa- tional interests of the country. During the past and preced- ing summers,however,some considerable interest was taken on the subject. Quite anumber ofdistricts were organizedunder theprovisions of our common school law, and a number of both public and private schools were taught in different parts of the country. I would recommend that the County Com- missioners be authorized to extend the tax for common school purposes to fivemills on the dollar. I'am happy to be able to congratulate the citizens of this Territory on the late arrival of our Surveyor General, Mr. Cartee, a gentleman of known and acknowledged abilities in hisprofession,from whom I understandtheinitiatorystepsforB- 2

This fact will be of special interest to our farm- ing population, as nothing is of greater importance to our agricultural interests than the speedy survey of our public lands . Mr. Street Introduced the following concurrent resolution, granting leave of absence to John M. Cannady . Resolved by the Legislative Council the House of Represen- tatives concurring, That John M. Cannady, County Commis- sioner of Boise County, I. T., be, and he is hereby granted leave of absence from the Territory of Idaho until the 15th of March, 1867. Having disposed of thisportion of the case, it remained only to consider whether the above statement of facts shows the existence of such an office, or the " holding " of such a " com- mission or appointment " by the claimant, as would bring him within the provisions of the eighth Section of the Organic A c t . 6 6 Your committee are clearly of opinion after an extended examination of the United States Statutes, and particularly of the Internal Revenue Law as it stands at present, that an As- sistant Assessorship of Internal Revenue is such an office," and is held by virtue of such " a commission or appointment " as disqualifies the holder thereof from becoming a member of the Legislative Assembly,so long as that "office" is filled, or that " commission" held " under the United States ." To sustain this position we refer to the Statutes at large, 39th Congress,page 2,from which we quote the followingAct, approved January 15th, 1866 : "Be it enacted, & c., That the Secretary of the Treasury is hereby authorized to appoint any Assistant Assessors of Inter- nal Revenue now provided by law." B y reference to the former law we find that each of the Assessors were authorized to divide his district, and appoint an Assistant Assessor. See Boutwell's Tax System, page 5, being Section 11 of " An Act to provide increased revenue from imports to pay interest on the public debt, and for other purposes." Approved June 30th, 1864. Whatever may have been the position of this officer prior to the passage of the Act of 1866, it is evident that Congress by depriving theAssessor of the power of appointment, and investing the responsible head of the Treasury Department with the authority to appoint these Assistant Assessors, de- signed to invest this office with more dignity and independence than a mere clerkship in the Assessor's office, which would follow from the position assumed by claimant's counsel. This view is further sustained by reference to "An Act making appropriations for the Legislative, Executive and Judicial expenses of the Government for the year ending the 30th June, 1867, and for other purposes." Approved July 23d, 1866. (Stat. at large, 39th Congress, page 205), in which the sum of ten millions eight hundred thousand dollars is appropriated " for salaries of Collectors,Assessors,Assistant Assessors,Rev- enue Agents, Inspectors and Superintendents of exports and drawbacks ." Here we have Assistant Assessors classified as officers in the same list with Assessors and other important officials of the Government. There is nothing in this classifi- cation to show that Congress failed to recognize the Assistant

J O U R N A L . 3 1 Assessor as any less an officer than the Assessor ; on the con- trary- the manner in which they are arranged in the Section proves that they are all regarded by Congress as officers. This view is further confirmed by reference to the amend- ments to the Revenue Law, Approved July 13, 1866, (amend- ments to Sec. 22, Stat. 39th Congress, pp. 104 and 105,-also p. 168, Sec. 60), which too long for quotation here- shows that the manner of settlement, amount and manner of pay- ment of salary, settlement with the Department, & c., are irreconcilable with the theory of exclusive local appointment and superintendence, which follows from the position that an Assistant Assessor has no status as an official. These important amendments of the present law should be borne in mind in considering the testimony of Messrs. Savage, Cummins and Geer as to the practice of the Department for- merly, in making appointments, accepting resignations, & c. The Assistant Assessor being regarded as an officer within the meaning of the Organic Act, the question arises, whether the disqualification resulting from the occupancy of such office attaches at the date of election, rendering him ineligible, and incapable of taking the office, or whether it is a personal dis- qualification which may be removed by resignation at any time subsequent to such election and before taking the oath of office in the Legislative Assembly . If the first of these positions be correct, then it necessarily follows that the candidate was unable to take that which the people endeavored to give, and the election was absolutely void, so far as Mr. Quivey was concerned. (Cushing : Law and Practice of Legislative Assemblies; p. 66 : " If an election is made of a person who is ineligible, that is incapable of being elected, the election of such person is absolutely void)." Your Committee do not feel called upon to speculate upon the consequences of such ineligibility in this instance, as we are satisfied from an examination of authorities that this disquali- fication is not of that nature which relates back to the date of election on the 13th of August last. The authorities make a wide distinction between that species of disqualification which amounts to ineligibility, and that disqualification which may be removed before claiming to assume the duties of such office. Cushing's Law and Prac. of Leg.Assemblies,page 28, sections 6 7 and 68 . Sec 68 reads : "When thelanguageusedis,that"no personshallbe aRepre- sentative or Senator," as in Constitution of the United States, Maine, and many others," shall be entitled to a seat," " or shall be amember unless," & c., as in the Constitution of Missouri :

3 2 C O U N C I L . in these cases the point of time to which the qualifications thus alluded to, are to be referred, is that of being qualified and as- suming the functions of a member." Again on page 31,same work, under the head of " Disquali- fying Offices and Employments," the same doctrine is laid down: "Disqualifications of this kind result from the holding of certain offices, or from the exercising of certain employments, commissions and professions,the functions of which are deemed incompatible with the proper discharge of the duties of a mem- ber, but of which one may divest himself at pleasure, and which are therefore relative rather than absolute. In general, as these disqualifications are not derived from the personal character of the individual, or inflictedby way of punishment, they do not render him ineligible, that is, incapable to be el- ected, but prevent him from assuming the functions of a mem- ber until they are removed. But this depends upon the lan- guage used in reference to each particular disqualification, and the time to which it relates. Thus where it is said, that no person holding a particular office, & c., " shall have a seat," " shall be a member," " shall at the same have a seat," " shall hold a seat," " shall be capable of having a seat," " shall be ca- pable of being a member," " shall be capable of holding any office," " shall act as a member," the disqualification relates to the time of assuming the functions of a member ; but where the following terms are used, namely " shall be incapable of being elected," " shall be eligible to a seat," " shall be eligible as a candidate for," " shall be ineligible," the disqualification relates to the time of election ." The words used in the Organic Act of this Territory are : " shallbe a member," and " shall hold any office." The first of these quotations is in exactly the language given by Cushing as one of the instances in which the question has been decided ; theother, " shall hold anany office," is very nearly the language in another case, and is fully within the scope of its reasoning. If these decisions, quoted and approved by Mr. Cushing, are good authority, as we believe them to be, this disqualification of Mr. Quivey is clearly one which refers to the time of ap- pearing to take upon himself the oath of office, and to enter upon the duties as a member of the Council. W e have been cited by counsel to the case of Searcey vs. Grow, reported in the 15th California reports, as holding a different doctrine from that advanced by Cushing ; but an examination of that casewill confirm the general doctrine laid down by Mr. Cush- ing. The language of the Organic Act of Idaho Territory, as shown before, is " shall be a member," and " shall hold any office." The word " eligible," does not appear in the 8th section of the Organic Act of this Territory. Had it been used in place of the lan- guage " shall be a member," " shallhold any office;" the elec- tion of Mr. Quivey would have been undoubtedly void, and the person receiving the next highest number of votes- provided he was otherwise eligible- would have been entitled to the seat as the Councilman from that county. (Cushing's Prac- tice, page 67, section 179). The authorities sustain this doctrine : That when the candi- date is ineligible, votes cast for him are thrown away ; and the candidate receiving the next highest number of votes is enti- tled to the office; but in case of disqualification occurring at the time of assuming the office which he is unable or unwilling to remove the office becomes vacant . The whole matter of the admission or rejection of the claims of Mr. Quivey to a seat in this body,in the opinion of your committee, resolves itself into this:- Has he resigned his commission as Assistant Assessor of In- ternal Revenue at any time prior to his presentation here to take the oath of office ? If he has legally resigned that office,then he is entitled to a seat in this body. If he has not,then he is undoubtedly ex- cluded by the 8th section of the Organic Act, and the office should be declared vacant. J O U R N A L . 5 3 Mr. Miller in the Chair . EXECUTIVE OFFICE , BOISE CITY, December 15th, 1866 . Gentlemen of the Legislative Assembly : } Your attention is invited to the great importance of a gen- eral system of retrenchment in Territorial expenditures. Having in my annual message recommended a system of rigideconomy as one of the remedies forthe present embar- rassed condition of our finances, I am pleased to learn that there is a bill now pending in the Council entitled an Act to relieve the Territorial Treasury, which contemplates the repeal of allActs and parts of Acts allowing increased compensation to be paid out of the Territorial Treasury to the Governor and Territorial Secretary. Having learned through highly respectable sources that there existed some delicacy with reference to myself, lest the re- peal of the law referred should be understood as having been prompted by personal feeling, permit me to assure you, gen- tlemen, that in the passage of the bill now pending, with a slight amendment, I shallbe happy to attribute to you a higher motive and a nobler object. I therefore beg of you to feel no embarrassment on my account, as individual interests should always be made subservient to the public good. If the Congress, in our Organic Act, failed to provide suf- ficient salaries for Territorial offices, it is unreasonable to ex- pect that our infant Territory will supply the deficit by tax- ation; and our remedy should be in memorializing Congress onthe subject, rather than resorting to our Territorial Treas- ury. The uniform practice of our Government has been to sustain the expense of Territorial Governments, and there is nogood reason why Idaho should be made the exception. The passage of the bill in its present form would have the effect to relieve the Treasury to the amount of $4,000 annu- ally. To so amend the bill as to repeal also an Act to amend anAct entitled an Act to provide increased compensation to officers in the Territory,approved Jan. 13th,1864,wouldhave the stillmore beneficial effect of relieving the the Treasury of $11,080 thus making a relief in the Treasury of $16,080, as willbe shown by the following figures : Extra compensation to Governor per annum...... $2,500 To Secretary . Whatever the seeming necessity may have been which, prompted the first Territorial Legislature to provide for in- creased compensation of the Legislative members out of the Territorial Treasury, it is certainly a matter of grave doubt whether such legislation is not entirely unauthorized by the OrganicAct. No. 9, with my objections to becoming a law. Said bill provides an oath of office for the members of the Legislature, all other officers elected or appointed within the Territory, and all attorneys admitted to practice in the Courts of this Territory, and re- peals the oath of office prescrided by the first Legislative As- sembly of the Territory of Idaho. Our Organic provides that allcivil officers shalltake an oath or affirmation "to support the Constitution of the United States, and faithfully to discharge theduties of their respective offices." Congressmay legislate over a Territory within the scope of

# Page 81^page=81
7 6 C O U N C I L . its constitutional power, and may establish a Territorial Gov- ernment and the form of the local government must be regu- latedby the discretion of Congress. (Dred Scott vs. Sanford, 19 How , p. 395). Congress may also legislate directly for a Territory. (See U. S. Statutes, vol. 12, pp.432, 501). The Constitution and laws of the United States, not locally inapplicable, are the laws of our Territory. Organic Act, section 13 . Our Territorial Government was created by Congress, and the oath of office required by the Organic Act, and such other oaths as may be deemed necessary, or ligitimately within the province of that body to prescribe. The passage of the bill now before me cannot do away with the existing laws of Congress. All civil officers, before enter- ingupon their official duties, are required to take an oath or affirmation, not by reason of its being upon the statutes of Idaho, but by reason of its being a law of Congress. Had this bill merely repealed the Act of the Legislature, passed December 28th, 1863, entitled " an Act to regulate official oaths," I should have signed itwithout hesitation. The differ- ence in the oath provided by this bill and the oath repealed is quite immaterial. The latter oath is stated in boththe affirm- ative and negative form, while the oath proposed is stated only in the affirmative form. The man who swears conscientiously to the oath provided in this bill, swears to all that is contained in that portion of the existing oath, and perjury will lie as far in the one case as in the other, and no further. The bill pro- vides that the oath, which is recited, shall be the only oath re- quired of members of the Legislature, District and County officers, attorneys, &c. Now, if Congress prescribes this oath of office for members of the Legislature, & c., she may at any time alter or change the oath or prescribe an additional oath, and the Legislature of Idaho cannot limit the power of Con- gress in such cases. I do not deem it proper that we should say to Congress, while yet a Territory, that we will tako such and such oaths and no other shall be imposed. It is doubtless quite proper that we should have upon our statutes some law defining official oaths,but in fixing this law we should be care- ful to incorporate all that is required by the laws ofthe United States, and in no case should we say that only such an oath should be required. The Organic Act prescribes the oath of office,and inthe laws of the United States,July 2d, 1862,we find the oath of allegiance. Every Federal officer is required to take both, and I am satisfied that the practice of the Gov- ernment has been to require members of Territorial Legisla- tures to subscribe to each of these obligations before drawing

Section four of the Organic Act says : " The Legislative power and authorityof said Territory shall be vested inthe Governor and Legislative Assembly." No doubts are enter- tained but that the act of Congress of July 2d,1862, required the executivebranch of the legislative power to take the oath of allegiance, and it would appear very strange that the other branch should be exempt from taking the same oath. The law which declares that one branch of the legislative power shall take a certain prescribed oath beforeentering upon the duties of office, and before being entitled to any of the salary or emoluments thereof, does without doubt extend to the other. As the billbefore me prohibits any other oathtobe required of any member ofthe Legislative Assembly except the one therein named,it is clearly in violation of the law of Congress referred to, as understood and interpreted by the de- partments, and in opposition to the practice adopted by the Government under saidlaw, on which account thebill is re- turned toyour honorable without my approval. Mr. Stevenson, from the Territorial Committee, presented a report upon the Specific Contract Law as follows : Mr. President- The committee to w h o m was referred the resolution : " Instructing the committee on Territories to inquire into the expediency of repealing the SpecificContract Law, now in force in Idaho Territory." Having had the same under consideration,beg leave to sub- mit the following report, in which are embodied the reasons for the repeal of the Act entitledan Act,etc., denominated the " Specific Contract," etc.,show that the Act of the Legislature passed at the session is in conflict with the legislation of Congress,which declares United States notes to be a legal ten- der at their face, in payment of all debts. In the issuance of Treasury Notes, (commonly called greenback,) provided for under the laws of Congress,it is provided that such notes shall be" lawful money, and a legal tender in payment of all debts public and private,withinthe United States except duties on imposts and dues and interest on the public debts." The constitutionality of this law of Congress has been ad- mitted by all the State Courts that have ever passed upon the law, and it would be surplusage to argue a question so univer- sally conceded. The law of Congress is very broad : It provides such notes shallbe a legal tender for all debts. An obligation to pay a certain sum of money is a debt ; to agree to pay a certain sum of gold coin is also a debt. No one willdispute that gold coin ismoney; judgments are debts; debts are the result of con- tracts,when thequantity is fixed and specified. These defin- itions are taken by allgoodjurists, and in a popular sense may bemore but not less comprehensive. Our Specific Contract Law provides, " That in an action on a contract or obligation in writing for the direct payment of money,made payable in any specified kind of money or cur- rency,judgment for the plaintiff, whether the same be by de- faultor after verdict, may follow the contract or obligation, and be made payable in the kind of money or currency speci

Now the obligation or contract contemplated in this law though it may be for gold coin is a debt inevery sense of the word. The law might aswellread that any contract or ob- ligation in writing for the payment of debts made payable in any particular kind of money or currency, & c., judgment shallbe rendered for the same kind of money, currency,&c. Our Legislature has undertaken to make a distinction be tween gold and legal tender notes,by denominating gold as money, and legal tender notes as currency. The weight of authority which is always considered a guide withjurists and legislative bodies,is against the decision of the Supreme Court of California. AINSLIE, President of the Council: Sir,-Herewith I return to your honorable body C. B. No. 37 with my objections. The Organic Act provides that all Township, District and County officers,not otherwise provided for, shallbe appointed or elected in such manner as shall be providedby the Governor and Legislative Assembly. The Governor and Legislative Assembly have providedby general law that all township, district and county officersshall be elected by the people, and have fixed the manner and time of holding elections. The sheriff, auditor and other county and township officers, with one or two exceptions, hold their offices for two years, and the term of office for every county officer begins on the first Monday in January ensuing his election . On the second Monday in August last a general election was held in all the counties in the Territory for the election of township, district and county officers, and all the counties in the Territory participated in said election. During the first ten days of this month, the county officers so elected can qual- ify and enter upon the duties of their several offices. In Ada County, (over which this Bill specially legislates,) persons claim to have been elected to the county offices of said county and have qualified and claim the right to said offices;s; and I am informed that steps have already been taken to determine the rights of the claimants. Whether those persons or others are entitled by law to the offices to which they claim tohave been elected, is not a question which I propose to discuss, or which the Legislature can settle by passing a law pretending to legislate the old officers into office two years longer or any definite time; nor can they settle the question by passing any law whatever ; such a question is for the Courts to decide.

# Page 145^page=145
1 4 0 C O U N C I L . The intention of C. B. No. 37 is to legislate the old officers into office in such a manner that the person claiming to be electedcannot go to the Courts to have their rights determined ; in short, it is to decide the legal rights of these parties by special legislation. The law is ample to settle the dispute be- tween the claimants of these offices. It is for the Judges of our Courts to see that the scales of justice be held with an even hand. The obligations of the Judge that he will dispense equal law and rights to all per- sons ; that he will faithfully and justly do equal and impartial justice to individuals and the public, and the great and mighty guarantees to that administration of justice which puts citizen upon an equal footing with citizen. An interference with the uniform administration of juttice, directing that administration aside from uniformity, so as to give to one man rights which must be denied to another, would at once be subversive of the liberty and security granted by the Constitution. This would emphatically be the case if any power but the Court was per- mitted to direct at pleasure the rules and measure of justice in specified cases. Who wouldbe safe if the Legislature were permitted to dictate the decision of causes pending : What would be the use of Courts under such a state of things ? They wouldbe mere instruments in the hands of others, and all their powers and usefulness would be paralyzed. Admit the principle, that the Legislature at pleasure can settle the rights of those claimants, who can look forward to the result. If this can be done, the tenure of every office is dependent upon the Legislature for its ratification. The people may elect,but the Legislature may defeat the election. If they can do so in one county they can do so in every county where the officers fail to suit a majority of the Legislature. In this way no election law can be made effectual. And again, I fail to see the reason for carrying these officers beyond the next election, unless the intention is to take the right of election en- tirely away from the people. Why not legislate them into office for five or six years instead of two years ? If the rule is good in one case it is good in the other. The office of a Legislature isto rear a system of laws, calcu- lated to secure and advance in the best possible manner the rights of all citizens of a State. Statutes are made either in affirmance of natural rights and duties and declarative of them, or are positive regulations for political reasons, respecting cer- tainmatters and things in themselves indifferent. In democraticgovernmentsjustice ought to be the principle, the publicgood the object,and reason and virtue the life and spiritof the laws. D. W. B A L L A R D.

The existing laws of the Ter- ritory provide for a District Attorney in each of theseDis- tricts. They are to be public prosecutors ; attend the different Territorial Courts within theirdistricts,and prosecute on be- half of the people all public prosecutions; give advice, etc.; and prosecute forfeited recognizance,and attend to such other duties as are requiredby law. They areelectedby the people every two years; receive certain salary and such fees for pros- ecuting in certain cases as are provided by law. This has been thesystem and policy of the Territory ever since the organ- ization. Iknow of no complaint against this system or any reason for changing the law in the 3rd Judicial District. The people ofAda, Owyhee and Oneida counties have not petitioned for any change or remonstrated or made any complaint against thegeneral policy of the Territory, or the district attorneys in their districts, nor have the people in any other district or county made complaint or asked for a change of the law in any manner whatever. The people have made the choice of their officers through the ballot box ; the elected officers have performed their duties ; the law has been universally acqui- esced in, and general satisfaction prevails. In fact I know of no law that has been more universally approved. C. B. No. 42 proposes to make three county public prosecutors in one district, and district public prosecutors in the other district. This bill also provides that in the counties named the County Commissioners shall appoint public prosecutors in the 1st and 2nd Judicial Districts ; the existing law still remains and pro- vides for the election of these officers by the people. It ispro- videdby the charter under which our Territory is organized, that township, district and county officers shall be appointed or elected. Township officers throughout the Territory should be either appointed or elected ; so also should the district and county officers be either elected or appointed. Shall we con- strue this law as a general law for the whole Territory, or for instance shallwe appoint a sheriff in one county and make the office elective in other counties. If we are to observe any rule at all,should we not make the

EXECUTIVE DEPARTMENT, BOISE CITY, I. T., Jannary 9th, 1867 . Hon. GEORGE AINSLIE, President of the Council : Sir- The election of a Commissioner by the Legislative As- sembly, for the purposes specifiedin CouncilNo. Bill65, instead of strengthening the hands of our Hon. Delegate in Congress by rendering him efficient aid in the discharge of his official duties, would, by inuendo at least, have the effect to cast sus- picion upon his integrity and ability. From his position he has the right to be heard not only on the floor of theHouse of Representatives, but also at the heads of Departments in our national Capital. Your honorable body has by resolution declared That Hon. E.D. Holbrook,ourpresent efficientDele- gate in Congress, is entitled to the entire confidence of the various Departments of the national administration, and that he enjoys the full and implicit confidence of the Legislature and the people of Idaho . IfourDelegate, to whom you have expressed such undoubted confidence, is unable from his position as our representative in Congressto secure the objects named in the bill, what good results might we expect from sending forward a citizenclothed with no authority whatever, and having no legalright,beyond what is enjoyed by all citizens in common, to be heard either inCongress or at the heads of the Departments ? A commissioner appointed by Congress to investigate the affairs named in the billwould occupy a position quite differ- ent from such a commissioner astherein provided for, from the fact that his report would go back to Congress under the sanc- tion of law, while the report of a Legislative Commissioner could have no legal right to consideration outside of our Terri- torial Legislature. Besides, there are now inWashington many safe and respect- able citizens from Idaho City, and other portions of ourTerri tory, who doubtless are at this time, willingly and without charge to our Territorial Treasury, heartily co-operating with our Delegate to secure not only the objects named in the bill, but allother measures contributing to the interests of Idaho. Therefore, not wishing to cast any imputations on the posi tion of our Delegate in Congress,the bill is returned toyour honorable body without my approval. D , W. BALLARD ,Governor,

THE COMMITTEE appointed to prepare Standing Rules for the government of the Legislative Council of the Territory of Idahowould respectfullyreportthe following Rules, and recom- mend their adoption : I. The Council shall choose,by ballot, one of the members to occupy the Chair who shall be entitled PRESIDENT OF THE COUNCIL, and who shall hold his office during the . Session thereof, unless he be removed therefrom by a vote of two-thirds of the members present. II . The President shall take the Chair at the hour to which the Council shall have adjourned ; shall immediately call the members to order, and on the appearance of a quorum shall cause the Journal of the preceding day to be read and cor- rected. III . He shall preserve order and decorum ; may speak to points of order in preference to other members, rising from his seat for that purpose ; and shall decide questions of order subject to an appeal to the Council by any member, and said appeal shall prevail when voted for by two-thirds of the members present. Gentlemen of the House of Representatives- Your resolu- tions requesting an explanation of the message transmitted on the 15th, are before me. I may have been unfortunate in the selection of terms to convey my meaning in that brief commu- nication, and shall endeavor to make myself understood in the present one. To give a categorical answer to your question, I will say that in returningjoint resolutions Nos, 2 and 3 with- out my signature, I did not either intend to oppose or veto them. The Organic Act says that every bill before it shallbe- come a law, shall be presented to the Governor, etc. etc., see sec. 6, Organic Act . A joint or concurrent resolution is not a bill, it does not be. B- 1 7

T r a e come a law- a resolution is an expression of the sense of the Legislative body on a given question, and inasmuch as the opinion of the Legislature is expressed as fully and is ascer- tained as competely without the signature of the Governor as with it, his signing a resolution could neither add to or detract from its validity. Noticing that the practice of my predecessors in this Terri- toryhad been to sign not only bills,but memorials, resolutions, etc., I inadvertently followed their precedent without consider- ation, and signed the two resolutions to which reference was made in my message of the 15th. But upon consideration becoming satisfied that my right to approve or reject the measures of the Legislative Assembly is confined to bills and does not embrace resolutions, I intended to so express myself in my former communication. Cushing in his law and practice of Legislative Assemblies, page 919, sec. 2377, says : The other papers besides bills which are required to be approved by the Executive are particularly specified in each constitution. The OrganicAct of this Terri- tory stands to us in the same relation that a State constitution would if we were a State, and as it does not specify any other T'papers except bills shallbe presented to the Governor, it fol- lows under the rule laid down, that such papers need not be submitted to the executive. That the oath prescribed in the Council Bill in question contains the substance of the oath required by the Organic Act, and in that respect is only declaratory thereof, and in no wise conflicts with any law of Congress knownto your Com- mittee. 4th. By making the endowment provided for in this Act, not only will the great interests of education be promoted but orphan asylums and hospitals, which have always been its twin sisters, will be established in our Territory under the control of the Sisters of Charity and Mercy,by whom the helpless and unprotected orphan and the victim of disease in all its various forms, willbe alleviated, nourished and sustained. And the endowments provided by this Act, and from which such immense benefits will be incurred, by advancing the educational, moral and physical condition of our people, will at the utmost require but ten per cent. of the proceeds of the thirty-sixth section of land aforesaid. The objection has been raised that this endowment isfor the benefit of a particular religious sect, at war with the spirit of republican institutions. This objection is, in our opinion, barely requires a proper elucidation to be completely removed. It shouldbeborne in mind that the Colleges, Universities and Academies that have been established in the newly organized States are endowed, and in fact supported from the proceeds of funds arising from the thirty-sixth section, and have almost universally been under the control of some particular denom- ination of Christians, mostly Protestant, and the argument, if argument it can be called, is much stronger against educational institutions under the control of Protestant denomirations than Catholic, for the reason that by the rules of Protestant institu- tions so established, allpersons attending thesame are required to listen to their spiritual teachings, while in Catholic institu- tions the persons attending are allowed fully and freely to attend such worship as they see fit, nor subjected to Catholic spiritual teachings. The State of California has made endowments to Protestant and Catholic educational institutions, without respect to the denomination of Christians controlling the same. Congress donated to the State of California five hundred thousand acres of land for purposes of internal improvement ; their Legislature transferred the same to the school fund , out of which liberal appropriations have been made regularly to the following institutions of learning in that State under the control of Catholics and the various Protestant denominations, which should be a sufficient answer to the objection that the Legislature should not now make this endowment, as the wants and interests of her people upon the subject of education are in many respects similar to our own . The peculiar situation of the people of our Territory, differ- ing as it does from the older States of the Union, is another vitalreasonin favor of the passage of the bill; ourpopulation is changing and unsettled, thereby operating most disadvan- tageously against the establishment of a thorough system of common schools ; the male population of our Territory,

The bill, in effect, provides for the issuance of bonds to the amount of thirty thousand dollars, to be prepared at the ex- pense of the Territorial schoolfund,bearing interest at the rate of ten per cent. per annum, payable to the order of the Right Rev. Francis N. Blanchet, Archbishop of Oregon, out of the proceeds of the sales of certain school lands,to enable his rev- erence and the Sisters of Jesus and Mary,of Portland,Oregon, and the Sisters of Providence, at Vancouver, Washington Territory, to establish and maintain schools within this Terri tory, upon an extensive scale, and in order that his reverence and his successors in office can legally take and administer the temporalities thus provided, they are constituted a corporation sole. The provisions of the Organic Act referred to in the bill are as follows : That when the lands in said Territory are sur- veyed,& c., sections numbered sixteen and thirty-six in each

J O U R N A L . 3 5 5 township in saidTerritory shall be,and the same are hereby reserved for the purpose of being applied to schools in said Territory, and in the States and Territories hereafter to be created out of the same . The question then arises, can the measure properly receive the sanction of this body. The solution of the question de- pends upon two propositions : First-Has the Legislative Assembly the legal authority to pledge those lands for the pur- poses contemplatedby theAct ? and Second-Is it politic to d o so ? The lands referred to in the bill are reserved for a special purpose ; the title thereto remains in the United States, and cannot be conveyed except by grant ; their disposition is sub- ject to such further regulations as Congress may provide. The Territory, as yet,have no right to them whatever- not even the title of a possibility coupled with an interest, and never will have until they are ceded to the Territory. Their present status is simply that they will be and are reserved from the operation of the land laws to be applied for school purposes. The manner in which that application willbe made depends wholly upon the laws of Congress. They may be sold and the proceeds loaned out and the interest alone applied for school purposes, or they may be granted to the Territory, but with such conditions annexed as to render the provisions of the Act in question wholly inoperative. In this view of the matter the proposed legislation would not only be premature but wholly void. Waiving,however,the objections suggested, and conceding that said lands are the subject of disposal by the Legislative Assembly, or that the proceeds thereof can be pledged for the purposes mentioned in the Organie Act, the question still remains as to whether the objects soughtby the passage of the bill under consideration legitimately answer those purposes. Those lands are reserved " for the purpose of being applied to schools " &c.; what schools are intended? certainly not those established and maintained by a purely sectarian creed, whose design and object is to prepare the mind to embrace the peculiar tenets of that creed! Such a construction would do violence to the spirit of our institutions , -would be in opposition to all precedent and evidently con trary to the intention of the Congress of the United States. Ever since the formation of our government the establish- ment of schools has been the subject of municipal authority. In every State and Territory general school systems have been adopted, the design of which has been to afford to every one, however poor or humble, the opportunities of an education uninfluenced by religious dogmas. Fanatical intermeddlers,it

# Page 361^page=361
3 5 6 C O U N C I L . is true,have inmany instances attempted to thwart that design, andhave greatly impaired their usefulness ; yet the system is acknowledged as an important part of the institutions of our country, and is comprehended within our general policy. These schools constitute an entire different class from those fostered by the church ; the one is established by law and sub- * ject entirely to municipal regulations ; the other by religious denominations and influenced by sectarian teachings ; the one is public and general, the other private and select; and when theAct of Congress contains the words " the schools, & c.," can there be any doubt as to what schools were intended. It certainlymeans those schools established by municipal authority as contradistinguished from those select schools established by private endowment and controlled by church rule. If this view be correct then the attempt to apply the proceeds of the sales of those lands in the manner proposed by the Act in question would be a misapplication of those funds, an abuse of the trust and a violation of authority. In the light of policy, what reason can be urged for the passage of this bill ? it is an acknowledgmnnt in the outset that our people are not capable of maintaining a system of schools common to every State and Territory in the Union, but that they have to invoke the wisdom and influence of the Right Rev. Archbishop of Oregon to establish schools among them and superintend the instruc- tion of their youth .And what would be the result ? our resources crip- pled; the encouragement and influence of the more wealthy patrons of our schools withdrawn, and their support left to the indigent portion of the community, we shall have accom- plished the establishment of one system and the destruction of the other ; we shall have secured in few favored localities select schools, accessible to the rich and fortunate, while the more remote portions will be deprived of all of its benefits ; we may adorn, beautify and improve the one locality while we neglect and desolate the other. We shall imitate the impru- dence of that savage who, when supplied with the means to obtain a suit of wearing apparel,expended it all in the pur- chase of a shiny hat,which he supported in strange contrast withhis old blanket and dilapidated breech-clout, displaying the fashionable gentleman atthe one end and theragged Indian at the other . W e shall have invaded with rude hand an ancient, time- honored system of education ; a system calculated to ramify the whole community; to permeate the entire body politic, and to extend to the remotest fragments of society a system liberal in design, republican in character, and which places

J O U R N A L . 3 9 3 Mr. Stafford, chairman of committee on Military Affairs, made the following report : To the Honorable the House of Representatives of the Legisla- ture of the Territory of Idaho : Your committee on Military and Indian Affairs respectfully submit the following report : Your committee have not deemed it necessary or advisable to recommend or bring forward any measure for the organiza- tion of the Militia of the Territory. No public arms have ever been received by the Territory, and we are not advised that any quota of the public arms has ever been assigned to Idaho Territory, although the very purpose of their distribution,under existing laws, is best subserved when the arms are put within reach of the population of new Territories, around and in which the hostile savage still lurks for pillage and murder. In the northern portion of the Territory peaceful relations exist between the whites and the Indian tribes settled there, which have not been interrupted since the organization of the Territory. This desirable and unusual condition is owing mainly to the fact that those tribes, the Nez Perces, Cœur d'Alenes, Pen d'Oreilles, & c., have been for a long time grad- ually adopting the pursuits of peace and habits of civilization, under good influences- acquired property and permanent hab- itations, and rely for a surer subsistence upon the cultivation of the soil and the raising of stock. But in Southern Idaho, throughout that portion of the Territory south of Snake River, your committee regret to say, a far different condition of af fairs has existed from the organization of the Territory, and stillcontinues. The scattered clans in all this region, known as the Shoshones or Snakes,inhabit a country for the most part destitute of timber and game, spreading into wide deserts,and affording them secure retreats in rugged mountains and deep canyons. Commencing theirdepredations upon the early emi- grants, they have continued their habits of theft and murder until the present time. Never having any fixed habitations, they acquire no property except by plunder, and hold none ex- cept for temporary subsistence and plunder. So, far from cultivating the soil or any arts of peace,they have to a great extent ceased to depend for food upon fish,grass seeds, crickets, roots, etc., and rely upon what they seize by murder and rob- bery on the public highways and frontier settlements. Their depredations upon the early mining population caused the ex- peditions of the winter of 1862-3 and spring of 1863 against them, which drove them from allthe region of country north of Snake River, and they have carried with them to the south- ern and south-western borders, in coalition with their cognate

Nothing, therefore, but vigorous war, that will push them to extremities of starvation or extermina- tion, can ever bring peace to our borders and security to our highways. The rapid progress of the contemplated railroad, and the fact that all the southern portion of the Territory will soon chiefly depend upon that for transportation of supplies and fa- cilities for travel, render it specially important that all these scattered predatory bands of Indians, in open hostility about our south-western borders,should be speedily suppressed. And in this connection,your committee take occasion to mention with much satisfaction,the fact that this subdivision,including the military operations against these Indians, has been placed under the control of Gen. The yearly receipts from the different sources of revenue are very small, being about one-third of the expenditures, and unless the Territorial Revenue is increased pro rata by addi- tional taxation to meet the current expenses,in a few years the Territory will be unavoidably and irretrievably insolvent. I would recommend that the property tax be increased from seventy cents to one hundred cents on the one hundred dollars. The rate of licenses is sufficient and adequate, but instead of the territory receiving only one-tenth of this source of revenue I would suggest an increase to twenty-five per cent.; this can be accomplished without materially affecting the interest of tax payers, and would result in placing the credit of the Terri- tory on a sound basis, the result of which would be that instead of warrants depreciating in their value, they would otherwise command a premium. In this connection I would recommend that the Committee of Ways and Means devote their serious attention to the finances : repealing, amending, and as the case demands, remodeling of the revenue law. Some means should be adopted whereby the Statutes already printed may be circulated among the officers of the various Counties, so that they may be enabled to perform their respect- ive duties in accordance with law . Heretofore this want has been seriously felt and has retarded in no small measure the collection of revenue . The revenue law, in regard to what kind of monies shall be paid and received for taxes, isplain and definite,but there isa disposition on the part of some of the Counties to make pay- ment in Legal Tenders at par, thus causing an uneven and uncertain currency in the Treasury,resultinginmuch injustice to warrant holders; and,again,gold dust ispaid and received wholly unfit for circulation,very oftenbeing composed in part ofsand,battery, and other foreignmatter. The demurrer was overruled in every particular, except that objec- ting to the complaint on the ground of its want of definiteness. On that point the demurrer was sustained, and the cause sent back to the District Court with leave to the Plaintiff to amend the complaint, and that the trial then proceed. An Act " to provide for funding the indebtedness of the Territory of Idaho," passed January 12th, 1866, Sec. 2, 4th line, " Treasurer or Receiver" should be stricken out and Con- troller substituted, as this is the proper department for claims against the Territory, to be audited and allowed. Also, same Act, Sec. 9, 2d line, should be amended so as to read " Trea- surer or Receiver and Controller," instead of " Treasurer or Receiver ." I would most heartily recommend, suggest and insist that the Treasurer be authorized to pay the salary of the Controller quarterly in cash. At present the law does not instruct a warrant to be drawn for the amcunt, and the payment is left entirely to the option and discretion of the Treasurer, who re- fuses to take any responsibility in the premises. As the Con- troller has to devote his whole time and attention to Territo- rial affairs, to the exclusion of all other business, he should have his salary increased in proportion to the importance of the office, say $3,000 per annum,to be paid quarterly in cash, which compensation would prove an incentive to the faithful performance of his duties. In conclusion, I would most respectfully state that the an- nexed statements are a full, correctand complete exhibit of the transactions of this department during my term of office. I have the honor to remain, Your most obedient servant, H. B. L A N E , Territorial Controller. B - 28

I have visited the Prison quarterly during the year, and found the prisoners well cared for, with responsible guard on duty as providedby law. The County Jail of Boise County isprobably as well adapted for temporaryary prison purposes as any County Jail in the Territory, comprising twelve cells of proper dimensions- the greatest defect being in the fence surrounding the Jail and used as Prison Yard, which is very defective, and prisoners may not be turned out without being closely guarded. The only escape during the year, that of Omesdale, occurring through this defection. Sec. 7th of Act referring to duties of Prison Commissioner provides that the Prison Keeper, under the direction of the Commissioner, shall,when it willconduce to the public interest, employ at hard labor all convicts in saidPrison. The provisions of this section have been inoperative, not- withstanding Mr. J. I. Crutcher has made repeated attempts to employ them. The law contemplates the manufacture of bricks,but we have not thought it conducive to the public interest to so employ them, as it would have involved an expense that the limited demand for that article in Idaho City did not justify. We also met with opposition in attempting to employ them in the mines, as that class of laborers are numer - ons,who are employed by the day. There arose a decided objection to convict labor coming in contact with theirs ; con- sequently we have been unable to realize any benefit from prisoners, or to make them in any way or part as intended by law- self sustaining. To the Council and House of Representatives ofthe Territory of Idaho : GENTLEMEN : It is a source of regret that the following Report will show our Common Schools to be in a very un- promising condition. We are still, in a measure, destitute of either Schools or School houses, and while every other branch of business is receiving its due share of attention, the interests of our Common Schools are in many places almost totally neglected. It will be seenby the tabular statement herewiththat reports have been received from only four Counties. Of the whole number of children between the ages of five and eighteen years, only a fraction over one-half are reported as having attended school during the year. Where they have attended, in most cases it has onlybeen for one quarter. In the report from Boise County the question was submitted whether the two-mill tax authorized by the last Legislatureto be levied for School purposes was to be understood as so much in addition to the then existing tax, or whether the 9th Section of Article 8 of the School Law abolished the tax authorized by the Legislature of 1864-5, which question is submitted to your honorable body for adjustment.
